MiniBoss.notes: The panel prints DR and SR where the maker's tooltips say 1st Decay Rate and 2nd Decay Rate. The six envelope sliders read higher as slower, because the code subtracts the slider from the register maximum before writing it to the chip. lines: Eight wavetable oscillators from the Namco 163 cartridge chip, sharing one morphable waveform
Sets how many of the eight oscillators the chip runs, 1 to 8; the chip divides its time between them, so more oscillators means a duller, grainier sound
Attenuates the voltage at the CHANNELS jack before it is added to the CHANNELS knob, and inverts it below zero
Sets how many oscillators the chip runs, through the attenuverter beneath the CHANNELS knob, 10V spanning all eight
Morphs between the five drawn waveforms, 1 to 5, interpolating sample by sample between neighbouring pairs
Attenuates the voltage at the WAVEFORM jack before it is added to the WAVEFORM knob, and inverts it below zero
Moves the waveform morph through its own attenuverter, 7V spanning all five waveforms
Sets the pitch of that oscillator, two and a half octaves either side of C4
Attenuates the voltage at that oscillator's FM jack before it is added to the pitch, and inverts it below zero
Sets the level of that oscillator, 0 to 15
Raises the pitch of that oscillator by a volt per octave; unpatched it reads the V/OCT jack of the oscillator above it, and the first oscillator reads 0V
Modulates the pitch of that oscillator, a full octave per 5V with the FM knob wide open; unpatched it reads the FM jack of the oscillator above it, and the first oscillator reads 5V
Scales that oscillator's AMP knob, 10V leaving it untouched and 0V silencing it; unpatched it reads the AMP jack of the oscillator above it, and the first oscillator reads 10V

Note — raising CHANNELS does not retune the oscillators, unlike the original chip, because the frequency register is computed without reference to the channel count

SuperSampler.notes: Parameter 8 and input 16 belong to the first voice's phase modulation, which the chip does not define; the widget skips both, so neither can be reached on the panel. No jack or knob on this module carries a name from the maker, and the panel art carries no lettering.

lines: Eight voices of the Sony S-DSP from the Super Nintendo, sharing the chip's noise source, echo unit and stereo mixer, on a panel the maker left unfinished
Sets the pitch of that voice, four octaves either side of C4
Switched on, the output of the voice above is fed into this voice's phase, which is the chip's own way of cross-modulating two voices
Switched on, that voice plays the chip's shared noise instead of its waveform
Sets the pitch of the shared noise, 0 to 31
Sets the left level of that voice, -128 to 127; below zero the signal is inverted
Sets the right level of that voice, -128 to 127; below zero the signal is inverted
Sets how long that voice's envelope takes to climb to full height, 0 to 15
Sets how long that voice's envelope takes to fall to the sustain level, 0 to 7
Sets the level that voice's envelope falls to before the sustain stage begins, 0 to 7
Sets how quickly that voice's envelope keeps falling once it has reached the sustain level, 0 to 31
Switched on, that voice is fed into the shared echo unit
Sets the echo delay time in sixteen steps of 16ms
Sets how much of the echo is fed back into itself, -128 to 127
Sets how much of the echo is mixed into that side of the output, -128 to 127
Sets the level of that side of the final output, -128 to 127
Sets that tap of the eight tap filter in the echo's feedback path, -128 to 127
Sets that voice's pitch at a volt per octave, added to its frequency knob
Modulates that voice's pitch, a full octave per 5V
Starts that voice on each rise past 2V and releases its envelope when the voltage falls back to 0V
Nothing in the module reads this jack; that setting can be changed only from its own knob or switch
Carries that side of the chip's stereo mix
Note — no voice sounds until a gate above 2V reaches its GATE jack, and each voice plays a short waveform built into the module rather than a sample you can load
Note — the panel carries no lettering beyond the title, which reads S-SMP (under development), and the maker named none of its jacks, so hovering one shows no tooltip
Note — only three of the module's jacks per voice are read at all: pitch, frequency modulation and gate. Every other jack on the panel is wired to nothing
Note — the module is monophonic. Every voltage is read from the first channel of its cable and the outputs carry one channel

lines: The three square wave tones and the noise generator of the Texas Instruments SN76489, the sound chip of the Sega Master System
Sets the pitch of that tone, two and a half octaves either side of C4
Sets what the noise runs at: fully anticlockwise it follows tone 3's frequency, and the three settings above that are fixed periods rising in pitch
Attenuates the voltage at that tone's MOD jack before it is added to the pitch, and inverts it below zero
Picks the noise flavour: one position gives white noise, the other the chip's periodic noise, which is pitched and buzzy
Sets the level of that voice, 0 to 15
Raises the pitch of that tone by a volt per octave; unpatched it reads the VOCT jack of the tone before it, and the first tone reads 0V
Moves the noise setting, each 2V raising it by one step, and does nothing until a cable is patched
Modulates the pitch of that tone, a full octave per 5V with the MOD knob wide open; unpatched it reads the MOD jack of the tone before it, and the first tone reads 5V
Flips the noise flavour set by the LFSR switch while it is above 2V
Scales that voice's AMP knob by the voltage here, 10V leaving the knob untouched and 0V silencing it; unpatched it reads the AMP jack of the voice before it, and the first tone reads 10V
Carries that voice's audio, hard clipped at 5V, with the audio of any earlier voice whose own output is unpatched added in
Note — the four outputs are chained: a voice whose output is left unpatched is summed into the next output along, so patching only NOISE gives a mix of all four

lines: The two pulse voices and the stepped saw of the Konami VRC6 cartridge chip
Sets the pitch of that voice, two and a half octaves either side of C4
Attenuates the voltage at that voice's MOD jack before it is added to the pitch, and inverts it below zero
Picks the duty cycle of that pulse, 0 to 7, from a sixteenth up to a full square
Sets the level of that pulse, 0 to 15
Sets the level of the saw, 0 to 63
Raises the pitch of that voice by a volt per octave; unpatched it reads the VOCT jack of the voice before it, and the first pulse reads 0V
Modulates the pitch of that voice, a full octave per 10V with the MOD knob wide open; unpatched it reads the MOD jack of the voice before it, and the first pulse reads 5V
Scales that voice's AMP knob by the voltage here, 10V leaving the knob untouched and 0V silencing it; unpatched it reads the AMP jack of the voice before it, and the first pulse reads 10V
Moves the duty cycle of that pulse, one step per volt; unpatched it reads the PW jack of the first pulse, which itself reads 0V
Restarts the saw from the beginning of its cycle on each rise past 0.02V
Carries that voice's audio, hard clipped at 5V, with the audio of any earlier voice whose own output is unpatched added in
Note — the three outputs are chained: a voice whose output is left unpatched is summed into the next output along, so patching only SAW gives a mix of all three
Note — the frequency knobs move the pitch by two and a half octaves either way, but their read-out in hertz is scaled in semitones, so the number shown while turning one is wrong
